Human Nutrition & Dietetics · Research Portfolio

Zainab Pakeeza

I am a Human Nutrition and Dietetics graduate from the University of Veterinary and Animal Sciences, Lahore, with a growing focus on nutrition research and evidence-based practice. Through my undergraduate training, I have worked across quantitative research, public health nutrition, clinical nutrition, sports nutrition and laboratory-based animal research. I enjoy turning nutrition questions into structured research—from developing questionnaires and collecting dietary data to analysing results in SPSS and communicating findings clearly. I am now seeking a Master's by Research opportunity where I can strengthen my research skills, learn from experienced researchers and contribute to work with meaningful implications for health and nutrition.

01 · About me

Built from nutrition, shaped by research.

I want the portfolio to show not only what I have studied, but how I have actually worked.

My academic training in Human Nutrition and Dietetics has given me a broad foundation in nutrition science, physiology, biochemistry, microbiology, immunology, clinical nutrition, public health and sports nutrition.

What I enjoy most is the research process: identifying a question, choosing an appropriate approach, collecting reliable information, working with data and presenting findings clearly. My experience includes a 400-participant undergraduate study, school-based nutrition intervention work and laboratory-based animal research.

Why Master's by Research?
I want to move from undergraduate research exposure to deeper research training, especially in study design, data analysis, scientific writing and practical research methods.

07 · Publication

One research project carried through to publication.

Publication information included in my academic portfolio.

Accepted · 2026

Effect of sweets intake on academic performance among university students, Lahore

Authors: Pakeeza, Z. et al. · Advances in Food and Nutrition

The project examined sweets consumption, academic performance, BMI, sociodemographic factors and mental health using questionnaire-based data and SPSS regression analysis.

Study scale400 participants planned; 391 surveys retained after data cleaning.
MethodsQuestionnaire development, data collection, descriptive statistics, simple and multiple linear regression.
Key findingThe unadjusted association between sweets intake and academic achievement was negative but not statistically significant.
